stem: What does Alertmanager do? Select all that apply.

options.text: Groups related alerts into single notifications
options.note: Right. Grouping is a core feature.

options.text: Routes alerts to receivers such as email, PagerDuty or Slack
options.note: Right. Through its routing tree.
Right. Both mute alerts, in different ways.
Prometheus evaluates rules. Alertmanager receives the resulting alerts.

explanation: Alertmanager handles alerts sent by clients such as Prometheus: de-duplicating, grouping and routing them to receivers, plus silencing and inhibition.
hint: One of these happens before alerts reach Alertmanager.

stem: A network partition triggers hundreds of per-instance database alerts in one cluster. Which feature turns them into a single compact notification?

options.note: Right. That's the docs' own example.
Silences mute alerts entirely for a set time. They don't summarise them.
Recording rules precompute series in Prometheus.
That controls re-sending, not combining alerts.

explanation: Grouping categorises alerts of a similar nature into a single notification. The docs configure grouping by cluster and alertname so a partition sends one notification.

stem: Which pairs correctly match an Alertmanager route setting with its default? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. The wait before the first notification for a new group.
Right. The wait before sending updates about a group.
Right. The wait before re-sending an unchanged notification.
group_wait defaults to 30s. 5m is group_interval.

options.text: Waiting a short time before the first notification for a new group, so related and inhibiting alerts can arrive
options.note: Right. An alert that resolves within it sends no notification.

options.text: How long a condition must hold before an alert fires
options.note: That's the for clause in a Prometheus alerting rule.

options.text: How often an unchanged notification is repeated
options.note: That's repeat_interval.
Silences have their own start and end time.

explanation: group_wait is how long to wait before sending the first notification for a new group, allowing alerts from other rule groups or servers, and inhibiting alerts, to arrive.
hint: It applies to the first notification only.

stem: Using the routing tree shown, where does an alert with labels service="mysql", team="frontend" go?
code:
route:
  receiver: 'default-receiver'
  group_by: [cluster, alertname]
  routes:
  - receiver: 'database-pager'
    matchers:
    - service=~"mysql|cassandra"
  - receiver: 'frontend-pager'
    matchers:
    - team="frontend"

options.text: database-pager, because continue defaults to false so routing stops at the first matching child
options.note: Right. The database route is listed first and matches.

options.text: frontend-pager, because team is checked before service
options.note: Children are checked in order, and the database route comes first.
Only with continue: true would it carry on to later siblings.
It matches a child route, so the root's receiver isn't used.

explanation: Alerts traverse child routes in order. If continue is false (the default), matching stops after the first matching child.
hint: Order matters, and continue is false by default.

stem: Using the routing tree shown, where does an alert with only service="redis" go?
code:
route:
  receiver: 'default-receiver'
  group_by: [cluster, alertname]
  routes:
  - receiver: 'database-pager'
    matchers:
    - service=~"mysql|cassandra"
  - receiver: 'frontend-pager'
    matchers:
    - team="frontend"

options.note: Right. An alert matching no children is handled by the current node.
The root route matches all alerts and handles unmatched ones.

options.text: database-pager, because redis is a database
options.note: The matcher is the regex mysql|cassandra, which redis doesn't match.
It has no team="frontend" label.

explanation: Every alert enters the root route, which matches all alerts. If an alert matches no child, it's handled by the current node's settings.

stem: A child route sets only matchers and receiver. What group_by and timers does it use?

options.text: It inherits them from its parent route
options.note: Right. Most optional settings are inherited if not set.
Children inherit unset values from the parent.

options.text: None. Alerts on it are never grouped
options.note: Inheritance supplies group_by.
Grouping and timing live on routes, not receivers.

explanation: Most optional route parameters (receiver, group_by, group_wait, group_interval, repeat_interval) are inherited from the parent node if not set.

stem: What does this inhibition rule do? source_matchers: [alertname="ClusterDown"], target_matchers: [severity="warning"], equal: [cluster]

options.text: While ClusterDown fires for a cluster, warning alerts for that same cluster are muted
options.note: Right. The equal list requires a matching cluster label.
Reversed. The source mutes the targets.

options.text: Mutes all warnings in every cluster permanently
options.note: Only while a matching source alert fires, and only for the same cluster.
Inhibition only mutes. It doesn't create alerts.

explanation: An inhibition rule mutes target alerts when a source alert exists, provided both have the same values for the labels in equal.
hint: Source mutes target, when the equal labels agree.

stem: You're doing planned maintenance on a database tonight and want no pages from it for 2 hours. What's the right tool?

options.text: A silence, created in the Alertmanager web UI (or amtool), for 2 hours
options.note: Right. Silences are manual, time-limited mutes.
Inhibition is automatic, triggered by another alert firing, not a manual time window.
That's heavy-handed and easy to forget to restore.
That only spaces out repeats. It doesn't stop the first page.

explanation: Silences mute alerts for a given time, based on matchers. They're configured in the Alertmanager web interface. Inhibition mutes alerts while other alerts fire.
hint: Manual and time-boxed, or automatic and alert-driven?

stem: You run three Alertmanagers for high availability. How should Prometheus be configured?

options.text: Point Prometheus at all three Alertmanager instances directly
options.note: Right. The clustered Alertmanagers de-duplicate between themselves.

options.text: Put a load balancer in front and point Prometheus at it
options.note: The docs say not to load-balance between Prometheus and its Alertmanagers.

options.text: Point it at one; the others are standby
options.note: Prometheus should send to every instance.
The Pushgateway isn't part of the alerting path.

explanation: It's important not to load balance traffic between Prometheus and its Alertmanagers. Point Prometheus at a list of all Alertmanagers. The cluster gossips silences and notification state.
hint: The docs explicitly warn against a load balancer here.

stem: In Alertmanager configuration, what is a receiver?

options.text: A named set of notification integrations, such as email_configs or slack_configs
options.note: Right. Routes point alerts at receivers by name.

options.text: The Prometheus server that sends alerts
options.note: Prometheus is the alert sender, not a receiver in this sense.
Matchers select routes. Receivers deliver notifications.
Silences mute alerts.

explanation: A receiver is a named configuration of one or more notification integrations, for example email, PagerDuty, Slack or webhook.

stem: How can you validate an Alertmanager configuration file?

options.note: Right. No running server is needed.
promtool checks Prometheus rule files.
That reloads Prometheus, not Alertmanager config.

options.text: It can't be validated before starting
options.note: amtool validates it.

explanation: You can use amtool check-config to validate an Alertmanager configuration file. You don't need a running Alertmanager server.
hint: Alertmanager ships its own command-line tool.
